tagline: Stories of faithful exiles in a pagan court and visions of beastly empires, both declaring that the Most High rules and that God's kingdom will outlast them all.
overview:
Daniel is two books in one cover. The first six chapters are court stories: a young man from Judah and his three friends, carried off to Babylon, are trained for the king's service and survive a series of crises. They refuse the king's food, interpret dreams no one else can read, walk out of a furnace, watch a proud king lose his mind and a drunken king lose his kingdom, and come up alive from a den of lions. The last six chapters are visions, told by Daniel in the first person, in which beasts rise from the sea, horns grow and break, angels explain what the prophet cannot grasp, and history marches toward a time of terrible persecution and then an end in which God's people receive the kingdom.

One conviction holds the halves together. Nebuchadnezzar learns it the hard way: "the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes" (4:25). Empires are real and they are dangerous, but they are temporary, and they answer to a throne higher than their own. The stories show how to live faithfully inside such an empire, serving it honestly while refusing to worship it. The visions show where the empires are going and promise that suffering saints will not be forgotten.

The book matters far beyond its size. It gave Jewish and Christian readers the language of apocalyptic hope, including the clearest Old Testament statement of bodily resurrection (12:2). It gave Jesus the title he used for himself more than any other, the Son of Man, drawn from the figure who comes with the clouds of heaven in chapter 7. And it has sustained believers under hostile governments in every century since, from the Maccabean martyrs to Christians under modern persecution.
author:
The book never names its author outright. Chapters 1 to 6 speak of Daniel in the third person, while chapters 7 to 12 are largely his own first-person account ("I, Daniel"), and Jewish and Christian tradition has taken Daniel himself as the source of the whole. Jesus refers to "the prophet Daniel" (Matthew 24:15), and most Christians through the centuries have read the book as the work of the sixth-century exile it describes.

Most modern critical scholars hold that the book reached its final form from an unknown author or circle of pious Jews (sometimes linked with the wise teachers of 11:33 and 12:3) during the persecution under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC. On that view the court stories are older traditions, perhaps from the Persian or early Greek period, and the visions were written for readers suffering under Antiochus, set in the mouth of a famous figure from the past, a practice common in Jewish apocalyptic writing of the period. Others hold a mediating view: that a historical Daniel stands behind the stories and some of the visions, but that the material was gathered, edited, and extended in later centuries.

Ezekiel names a righteous and wise Daniel alongside Noah and Job (Ezekiel 14:14, 20; 28:3). Some identify him with the Daniel of this book; others note that the spelling differs slightly and think Ezekiel means an ancient figure of legend, possibly the Danel known from texts found at Ugarit.
date:
The date of Daniel is one of the most debated questions in Old Testament study, and the debate is really about how the visions work.

The traditional view places the book in the sixth century BC, written by or from Daniel, who lived from the first deportation (about 605 BC) into the reign of Cyrus (after 539 BC). Its defenders point to the book's own claims, to Jesus' reference to Daniel as a prophet, to the book's knowledge of sixth-century details (such as Belshazzar, whose existence and role as co-regent were long doubted and are now confirmed by Babylonian texts), and to the conviction that God can reveal the future. They also note that copies of Daniel were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the oldest from the late second century BC, which leaves little time for a book written in the 160s to be copied and treated as Scripture.

The critical view dates the book, in its final form, to about 167 to 164 BC. Its defenders argue that chapter 11 traces the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids in precise detail down to the persecution of Antiochus IV, then becomes vague and does not match what happened at his death in 164 BC, which suggests a writer living just before that death. They add that the book's Aramaic and some loanwords (including Greek names for musical instruments in chapter 3) fit a later date, that some details of the sixth-century setting are puzzling (such as Darius the Mede), and that the Hebrew Bible places Daniel among the Writings rather than the Prophets. An old version of this argument goes back to the pagan philosopher Porphyry in the third century AD, whom Jerome answered in his commentary on Daniel.

Mediating positions hold that the stories and some visions come from the exile or the Persian period and that the book was completed later. Readers who share a firm confession about God's rule and Scripture's authority differ on this question.
setting:
The stories are set in the royal courts of Babylon and Persia. Nebuchadnezzar II (605 to 562 BC) made Babylon the dominant power of the Near East, defeating Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, taking captives from Judah that year and again in 597 BC, and destroying Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. After his death the empire weakened. Its last king, Nabonidus, spent about ten years at the oasis of Tema in Arabia and left his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon. In 539 BC Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian, whose empire would rule the region for two centuries until Alexander the Great conquered it in the 330s BC.

The visions look further ahead, to the kingdoms that would follow Babylon and above all to the Greek period. After Alexander's death in 323 BC his empire split among his generals. Two of their dynasties, the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria, fought over Judea for more than a century. In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes banned Jewish worship, set up a pagan altar in the Jerusalem temple, and put faithful Jews to death. The revolt led by Judas Maccabeus retook and rededicated the temple in 164 BC, the event remembered at Hanukkah. On either view of the date, these events stand behind chapters 8 and 11, and the book's first readers under Antiochus found in it both a warning and a promise.
purpose: Daniel was written to strengthen God's people when they had no political power and every reason to think their God had lost. The stories model a faith that can serve a foreign empire with excellence and still refuse to bow to its gods, and they show God able to protect his servants or to be trusted even if he does not (3:17-18). The visions put persecution inside a larger frame: the beasts have their time, their time is measured, the heavenly court sits, and the kingdom is finally given to the saints of the Most High. The book calls for endurance and wisdom rather than panic, and it holds out resurrection as the answer to martyrdom (12:2-3). Its readers were exiles in Babylon, Jews under Persian and Greek rule, and the Maccabean generation facing death for their faith, and the book has spoken to every community in a similar place since.
story: Daniel sits in the exile, the great crisis of the Old Testament. Kings and Chronicles tell how Judah fell; Jeremiah and Ezekiel explain why; Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther tell of the return and of life under Persia. Daniel covers the whole period of Babylonian captivity, from the first deportation (1:1) to the first year of Cyrus (1:21), and then looks beyond it to centuries of rule by foreign empires. It answers a question the exile raised: if the house of David has fallen and the temple is gone, is God still king? Daniel's answer is yes, and it widens Israel's hope from a return to the land to a kingdom that fills the whole earth (2:35) and a resurrection beyond death. That wider hope is the one the New Testament picks up.
christ:
Daniel shaped the vocabulary of the Gospels. Jesus announced that "the kingdom of God is near" (Mark 1:15), and Daniel is the Old Testament book most concerned with the kingdom that God himself sets up (2:44; 7:14, 27). Jesus called himself the Son of Man more than by any other title, and at his trial he joined Psalm 110 to Daniel 7:13, telling the high priest that he would see "the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). He spoke of "the abomination of desolation" described by Daniel (Matthew 24:15). Revelation borrows Daniel's beasts and its description of the Ancient of Days for the risen Christ (Revelation 1:13-14; 13:1-2).

The stories also carry a pattern the gospel completes: a faithful servant condemned by the powers, placed in a sealed pit, and brought out alive, with a pagan ruler then confessing God's kingdom (chapter 6). That likeness is a pattern, not a prediction, but the early church saw it clearly. Daniel's hope of resurrection (12:2) and of a kingdom given to a human figure from the presence of God find their fulfillment, in Christian confession, in the risen Jesus.
reading:
Read Daniel as two kinds of writing. The court stories are narratives with the shape of tales about wise courtiers: a crisis, a failure of the pagan experts, the rise of the Jewish hero, and a king who praises God. The visions are apocalyptic, a genre in which a seer receives revelation through dreams and symbolic images (beasts, horns, numbers), usually with an angel as interpreter, and in which history is shown from heaven's side and moving toward God's final judgment. Apocalyptic symbols are not code to be cracked line by line against the news. They are pictures meant to show what powers are like and who finally rules them, and Daniel often supplies its own interpretation.

Notice that the book is written in two languages. Daniel 1:1 to 2:4a and chapters 8 to 12 are in Hebrew; 2:4b to 7:28 is in Aramaic, the common language of the empires. The switch does not match the division between stories and visions, so chapters 2 to 7 form their own unit. Chapters 2 and 7 both describe four kingdoms followed by God's kingdom, and they frame the Aramaic section.

The four kingdoms are read in two main ways. The older view, found in Jerome and held by most Christian interpreters until modern times and by many today, identifies them as Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome. The other view, held by most critical scholars and some others, identifies them as Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, with the fourth beast's little horn as Antiochus IV. Futurist readers add that the fourth kingdom, or its final stage, reaches into the end of history. The Greek versions of Daniel include further stories (Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah with the Song of the Three Young Men), which Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and Protestant Bibles place in the Apocrypha.

structure.title: Faithful in Babylon
structure.summary: Daniel and his three friends are taken into the king's service, refuse the royal food, and are given wisdom by God. The chapter, in Hebrew, introduces the characters and the setting of the whole book.

structure.title: The Aramaic chapters: kingdoms and the kingdom of God
structure.summary: Stories of dreams, a furnace, a humbled king, writing on a wall, and a lions' den, framed by two visions of four kingdoms (chapters 2 and 7). Chapter 7 begins the visions but belongs to this Aramaic unit.

structure.title: The ram and the goat
structure.summary: The book returns to Hebrew with a vision of Persia and Greece and a little horn that attacks the sanctuary, widely identified with Antiochus IV.

structure.title: Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
structure.summary: Reading Jeremiah's seventy years, Daniel confesses Israel's sin, and Gabriel answers with a prophecy of seventy weeks of years.

structure.title: The final vision
structure.summary: A long revelation of wars between the kings of the north and south, the persecution of the faithful, and the promise of resurrection at the end.

themes.title: The Most High rules
themes.body: Every chapter presses the same claim: God gives kingdoms and takes them away. Nebuchadnezzar is made to confess it (4:34-37), Belshazzar ignores it and dies (chapter 5), and Darius decrees it (6:26). The visions show the same truth on a larger canvas. Empires rise like beasts from a churning sea, but a court sits in heaven and their dominion is taken away.

themes.title: Faithfulness in exile
themes.body: Daniel and his friends learn Babylon's language and literature, take Babylonian names, and serve its kings with integrity. They draw the line at worship and at what would defile them. The book offers a model for living as a minority under a power that does not share your faith: neither withdrawal nor surrender, but loyal service with a limit.

themes.title: Wisdom that comes from God
themes.body: The wise men of Babylon, with their omens and dream manuals, fail again and again. Daniel succeeds not because he is cleverer but because God "reveals the deep and hidden things" (2:22). Wisdom in Daniel is both learning and revelation, and in the later chapters it is the calling of the wise to understand the times and to lead many to righteousness.

themes.title: Suffering, endurance, and resurrection
themes.body: The visions are honest about persecution: the saints are handed over for a time, the sanctuary is trampled, and the wise fall by sword and flame. Deliverance does not always come before death. The book's final answer is resurrection, the dead awakening to everlasting life or disgrace, and the promise that the faithful will shine like the stars (12:2-3).

themes.title: The kingdom given to the Son of Man
themes.body: Human empires are pictured as beasts; God's kingdom is given to one like a son of man, a human figure who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion, and it is shared with the saints of the Most High (7:13-14, 27). The New Testament hears this as the heart of Jesus' own claim.

keyChapters.why: Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream sets out four kingdoms followed by a stone that becomes a mountain and fills the earth, the kingdom God himself establishes.
Three young men refuse to worship the golden statue and are delivered in the furnace, the book's classic picture of faith that will not bow.
Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration, told in his own voice, teach that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men and humbles the proud.
Daniel keeps praying despite the king's decree and is delivered from the lions, a story of quiet, costly faithfulness.
The vision of four beasts and the Ancient of Days, where one like the Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom, the source of Jesus' favorite title for himself.
Daniel's prayer of confession and the prophecy of seventy weeks, one of the most debated passages in the Bible.
The book closes with the clearest Old Testament promise of the resurrection of the dead.
